8803704.twitter_share_message: “This references back to the Scylla and Charybdis episode wherein Stephen is discussing Hamlet, “…” —@Genius

children: This references back to the
Scylla and Charybdis

episode wherein Stephen is discussing Hamlet, “the distracted” or absentminded beggar. The allusion is to a Hamlet soliloquy in which he asks whether his own inaction is caused by “bestial oblivion,” or by a dull or cowardly thoughtlessness. Since both thought and action in this episode are bestial, “dull” and “cowardly” perhaps are better indictments of Stephen in the previous episode. Hamlet’s tendency to forget his purposes as avenger of his father’s murder, is similar to Stephen’s propensity toward distraction as to his purposes as literary creator, as demonstrated this evening through mind-numbing alcohol and sex, something paralyzing many young Irishmen, but is especially unfortunate with one, who, like Hamlet, has a supposedly unique role to play, requiring action, not degenerate inaction.
Much of Joyce’s great talent is due to a nearly encyclopedic memory and ability to focus, to avoid distraction. Something that becomes very apparent to the
Ulysses
reader is how critically needful those gifts are for himself.

children: Hamlet again. This time it’s from the mini-play
The Mousetrap

. What we’ve just seen is intentionally over-the-top vulgar and cruel. Hamlet advises the cast caution against overacting. “For anything so overdone is from [contrary to] the purpose of playing, whose end, both at the first and now, was and is, to hold, as ’t were, a mirror up to nature; to show virtue her own feature, scorn her own [nature’s] image and the very age and body of the time his form and pressure.” The scene just endured here in
Circe

is seemingly overwrought, and laden with inflated distaste so as to hold up a mirror to, and scorn, unconstrained nature, the image of that age in Ireland, the form of the times. We can conclude, then, that if what has been displayed in the scene is not exaggerated, but is intended as an accurate portrayal of contemporary Irish culture, then it is not, in fact, overacting.

From Middle High German vrouwenzimmer; Frau (“woman”) +‎ -en- +‎ Zimmer (“room”). Compare Danish fruentimmer and Swedish fruntimmer.

The Charge of the Light Brigade
Half a league, half a league,
⁠Half a league onward,
All in the valley of Death
⁠Rode the six hundred.

Their’s not to reason why,
Their’s not to make reply,
Their’s but to do and die,
Into the valley of Death
⁠Rode the six hundred.
Cannon to right of them,
Cannon to left of them,
Cannon in front of them
⁠Volley’d and thunder’d;
Storm’d at with shot and shell,
Boldly they rode and well;
Into the jaws of Death,
Into the mouth of Hell,
⁠Rode the six hundred.
Flash’d all their sabres bare,
Flash’d all at once in air,
Sabring the gunners there,
Charging an army, while
⁠All the world wonder’d:
Plunged in the battery-smoke
Fiercely the line they broke;
Strong was the sabre-stroke;
Making an army reel
⁠Shaken and sunder’d.
Then they rode back, but not,
⁠Not the six hundred.
Cannon to right of them,
Cannon to left of them,
Cannon behind them
⁠Volley’d and thunder’d;
Storm’d at with shot and shell,
They that had struck so well
Rode thro' the jaws of Death,
Half a league back again,
Up from the mouth of Hell,
All that was left of them,
⁠Left of six hundred.
Honour the brave and bold!
Long shall the tale be told,
Yea, when our babes are old—
⁠How they rode onward.
